records.current_summary:
Anti-discrimination law here expressly covers gender identity and gender expression in employment, housing and public accommodation, the last directly traveller-relevant for hotels, restaurants and venues, and the state's highest court enforced that coverage in May 2026 by ordering a hospital to resume the youth gender-affirming care it had suspended under national pressure. A July 2026 national risk map lists this state among the country's most protective, citing insurance-coverage mandates and refuge protections for people fleeing restrictive laws elsewhere.

The 2025 national document and passport restrictions apply here as across the country.

prison_adds.title: Colorado Department of Corrections (Wikipedia) — Transgender inmates section
prison_adds.summary: Wikipedia article (fetched, HTTP 200) whose 'Transgender inmates' section documents the state's actual placement practice: a 2019 class action on behalf of transgender women held in men's prisons alleged CDOC subjected them to sexual and physical violence and denied medically necessary care, and a court-approved 2024 consent decree in Denver District Court (Raven v. Polis) required CDOC to expand health care and create voluntary specialized housing — a 100-bed unit at the men's Sterling facility and an integration unit at the women's prison — and to pay about $2.1 million to roughly 400 class members without admitting liability. It also records a 2019 settlement (Lindsay Saunders-Velez, $170,000) over the safety of a transgender inmate held in a men's prison. Placement axis: no identity-based-housing statute; trans women were historically held in men's prisons, with relief achieved through litigation and consent decree rather than a baseline housing rule.

records.current_summary:
New Brunswick is the clearest Canadian case of a provincial government reversing course on trans rights within one election cycle. Policy 713 (2020) originally protected 2SLGBTQIA+ student privacy and inclusion. In July 2023, the Higgs government amended it to require parental consent for under-16 name/pronoun use, triggering protests outside the legislature. The Holt government reversed the amendment on 19 December 2024, effective 1 January 2025: parental consent is now "encouraged but no longer required" for the informal use of chosen names and pronouns by students of any age (it remains required for formal use in official records for students under 16), with a "presumed capacity" concept based on child-and-youth-advocate recommendations. The revised policy text extends its application to the whole school environment, including "visiting professionals, student teachers, parents, volunteers, and visitors", so current school rules technically reach non-residents present in classrooms.

Deviation: 0.02 below the national score of 0.86. The reversal is a strong positive institutional response — a government that legislated against trans students repealed the provision after one term. The residual signal is the demonstrated capacity for hostile policy within an election cycle and the 2023 protest period, which create a slightly higher baseline of political volatility than provinces that never legislated against trans people. No street-level disruption of public expression events was documented.

Compared to Alberta (0.76) and Saskatchewan (0.79), New Brunswick is materially higher: it did not use the notwithstanding clause, and its hostile policy was reversed rather than immunised from judicial review. Compared to the national score, the gap is small and time-sensitive — the current effective policy is protective, and further reversal would bring New Brunswick to or above the national level.

prison_adds.title: Transgender rights in Canada (Wikipedia; Prisons section)
prison_adds.summary: Wikipedia 'Transgender rights in Canada', Prisons section (accessed 4 Oct 2026): at the federal level the Correctional Service of Canada (CSC) permits gender-diverse offenders to request placement or transfer to a men's or women's institution aligned with their gender identity or expression, regardless of anatomy or the sex marker on their identification documents; requests are assessed individually and may be refused where an unresolved 'overriding health or safety concern' exists under CSC's 2022 gender-diversity policy. The article reports that as of 2025 CSC recorded 90 self-identified transgender women in federal custody - 73 housed in men's institutions and 17 in women's - and that between fiscal years 2017-18 and 2024-25 CSC received 129 placement/transfer requests from people assigned male at birth to women's institutions (35 approved, 72 denied, 22 withdrawn). Provincial correctional policies vary and the article does not document a New Brunswick provincial-jail placement rule; the federal policy is the framework a trans prisoner in federal custody in New Brunswick stands under. The Correctional Investigator has criticised the policy's unclear 'health or safety' override criteria and the lack of a dedicated abuse-reporting mechanism.

records.current_summary:
The capital recorded the highest transfeminicide toll in the country in 2024 — 17 LGBT+ homicides, of which 11 were trans women — and remains among the highest-count states in 2025. The raw violence data is a negative signal for a visitor, though part of the elevated count reflects the capital's superior reporting infrastructure rather than proportionally higher danger.

Counterbalanced by the strongest institutional response of any Mexican state: transfeminicide was made a distinct crime in July 2024 (“Ley Paola Buenrostro”, the second state to do so); a dedicated Transfeminicide Investigation Unit created in December 2024 covers all violent deaths of trans women; a prosecutor's protocol (Acuerdo FGJCDMX/04/2025) requires feminist-context investigation with immediate-action deadlines; and a new Gender Police launched in August 2025 with 30 patrol units. For a visitor assaulted in the capital there is trained machinery to investigate, where other jurisdictions have none. Modestly above the national score (0.55): the protective and investigative framework is the strongest in Mexico and materially changes what a visitor who encounters violence or discrimination faces after the fact, even though the pre-violence risk data is the country's worst.

prison_adds.title: LGBTQ people in prison (Wikipedia; Mexico/CDMX section)
prison_adds.summary: Thin: Wikipedia's 'LGBTQ people in prison' article, Mexico section (accessed 4 Oct 2026), documents only one Mexico City prison-system policy: in July 2007, through the efforts of the (capital's) National Human Rights Commission (CDHDF), the Mexico City prison system began allowing same-sex conjugal visits on the basis of a 2003 law banning discrimination based on sexual orientation, with the visitor not required to be married to the inmate and the change applying to all Mexico City prisons. The article contains no data on trans-prisoner housing placement in Mexico City (birth-sex vs identity placement), special units, or segregation practice; the country-level MEX record carries the same finding.

records.current_summary:
For a visitor the risk in Minas Gerais is violence-exposure, patterned over two years: the jurisdiction ranked 2nd nationally in 2024 with 12 killings and tied for the top in 2025 with 8; the consistency of appearing in the top two every year signals a structurally elevated environment. Against a population of ~21 million, the 2025 rate of ~0.38/million sits at the national average, but the pattern — not the rate alone — is the distinguishing risk factor.

The 68%-outside-capitals finding of the 2024 dossier implies added danger away from the capital for a visibly trans visitor moving through the interior. No state-specific legal restriction or unique ordinance was identified; the national framework applies.

prison_adds.title: G1 - Governo publica portaria com direitos para presos gays e travestis (Portaria SDH/PR 419/2014)
prison_adds.summary: G1 (17 Apr 2014): the Secretaria de Direitos Humanos da Presidência da República published a federal portaria setting where LGBT prisoners are housed across Brazil's prison system, which applies in Minas Gerais' state system: transsexual men and women must be forwarded to female prison units; gay and travesti prisoners held in male prisons must be offered specific conviviality spaces; LGBT inmates may use their social name (which must appear in the admission record) and choose male or female clothing. No sanctions are provided for non-compliance, and the report documents no Minas Gerais-specific implementation, wing, segregation practice or case.

records.current_summary:
For a trans visitor the documented signal in Paraíba is exposure, not law: the dossiers' consistent victim profile — young, Black, poor, 97% travestis and trans women, most killings in public spaces at night and outside state capitals, frequently mis-recorded by authorities — concentrates risk on people who present visibly in public. The jurisdiction recorded 4 killings of trans and travesti people in 2025, mid-pack in the dossier's state ranking, within a national total of 80.

No jurisdiction-specific statute, ordinance or enforcement policy affecting trans people was found in the audited sources; the national framework applies uniformly.
